paras: The attempted lynching of Albert Bulow took place at the Morrison County jail in Little Falls, Minnesota, in early December 1888, when about 150 people came before dawn to seize Bulow, who was charged with murder. Sheriff Rasicot, warned by telegram, had already taken Bulow and a second prisoner, Frank Randall, out of the jail, and the crowd left after searching it. Minnesota and out-of-state papers reported it as a sheriff saving a murderer from a mob.

Bulow was arrested at Verndale in late November, charged with shooting Frank Eich near Royalton on November 24, and a statement printed as his confession said the two had quarreled over unpaid wages. According to a Little Falls telegram, people in the south of the county near the scene had threatened to lynch him, and local authorities organized a force to back the sheriff. On December 3 Bulow pleaded not guilty, waived examination and was held for the grand jury in March. Randall, described as the killer of a man named Ziegler, was held in the same jail.

The St. Paul Daily Globe's Little Falls correspondent, writing under a December 5 dateline, reported an unusual influx of strangers the previous day. After a telegram warning, Sheriff Rasicot and Deputy William Rasicot shackled the two prisoners together and drove away in a carriage about 6 o'clock that evening. At 4:30 the next morning a crowd of about 150, in twenty-six wagonloads from St. Cloud, St. Wendel, Buckman and other towns in Morrison, Benton and Stearns counties, demanded entry from Deputy Sheriff John Sands.

When the crowd refused to believe the prisoners were gone, the jailer admitted a delegation of ten, who searched the jail and found it empty, and the crowd then dispersed. The correspondent wrote that Bulow was "the special object of vengeance" and that Randall was not wanted. A follow-up letter said the sheriff had recovered the slip-knotted rope with which the crowd "proposed to hang Bulow."

The prisoners were found to have been taken by team across country to the Brainerd jail, and Randall was to be returned to Little Falls because, in a Brainerd dispatch's words, "his life is not wanted." Over the next days men from Royalton and friends of Eich at Brainerd were reported reconnoitering that jail, and on December 9 the sheriff left with Bulow in irons on the noon train. A Brainerd dispatch by then identified Bulow as Charles Hassel, a former Northern Pacific fireman, and a December 11 report from Little Falls said parties were still "ready to lynch him" amid "great excitement."
No arrest of anyone in the crowd and no report of Bulow's trial were found in the coverage.

The Globe headlined its first report "Saved by the Sheriff" and called the crowd "would-be lynchers" whom the sheriff had outwitted, while calling both prisoners "murderers" and saying that, had Bulow been found, "justice would have been summarily meted out" to him. Its later items kept that line, closing on the assurance that "law will prevail."

A Brainerd wire dated December 6 ran on December 7 in the Wichita Eagle as "To Avoid a Lynching" and in the Fort Worth Daily Gazette as "To Escape a Mob," and on December 13 in the Emporia Weekly News as "A Sheriff Saves a Murderer," each noting that Bulow "was scared almost to death." Minnesota weeklies such as the Morris Tribune and the Sauk Centre Herald gave it one sentence in their "Minnesota News Notes," and the Emmons County Record in Dakota reprinted the Globe story on December 28 as "Attempted Lynching Frustrated." No paper mentioned the race of the prisoners or the crowd.

The Globe's dispatch dated December 5 places the crowd at the jail that morning, while the Emmons County Record's rewrite moves the influx to Wednesday, December 5, and the raid to the next morning. The Brainerd wire, which says the prisoners arrived there on the morning of December 6 after a night drive, fits the later date, but the Globe's same-day local report is the more direct source.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Albert Bulow
bases: A crowd of about 150 came to the Little Falls jail before dawn to seize and hang a prisoner accused of murder and left only after finding he had been removed (A3, A4).

No one was killed: the sheriff removed Bulow and Randall before about 150 would-be lynchers reached the jail, so this was an attempted lynching on the pretext of punishing an accused murderer (A3, A4, A5).
The Little Falls account in the Globe (A3, A4) and a separate Brainerd wire (A5) agree that the sheriff moved the prisoners to escape a mob; the News Notes item (A10) also reports it.

accounts.label: Little Falls correspondent (St. Paul Globe)
accounts.gist: Warned by telegram, the sheriff left with both prisoners about 6 p.m.; at 4:30 the next morning about 150 people demanded entry, ten searched the jail, and the crowd left.

accounts.label: Brainerd wire
accounts.gist: To escape a mob, the sheriff brought both prisoners to the Brainerd jail 'this morning' (Dec. 6) after a night drive across country; Randall was to go back because 'his life is not wanted'.

accounts.label: Minnesota News Notes
accounts.gist: Twenty-six wagonloads of lynchers demanded Bulow at the Little Falls jail, but the sheriff had hidden him.

framing.detail: The Globe's local reports cast the sheriff as 'too sharp for the would-be lynchers' and said 'law will prevail', while still calling Bulow 'the murderer' and saying 'justice would have been summarily meted out' had he been found.
Papers outside Minnesota ran the Brainerd wire under 'To Avoid a Lynching', 'To Escape a Mob' and 'A Sheriff Saves a Murderer', stressing that Bulow 'was scared almost to death'.
The syndicated Minnesota News Notes gave the episode one sentence, calling the crowd 'lynchers' and Bulow 'the murderer'.

versions.value: Prisoners removed about 6 p.m. the day before the Little Falls dispatch dated Dec. 5; crowd at the jail at 4:30 a.m. on Dec. 5
Influx noticed on Wednesday, Dec. 5; crowd at the jail the next morning
Night flight by team ending at the Brainerd jail on the morning of Dec. 6

conflicts.note: The Globe's same-day local dispatch (A3) is the best evidence for Dec. 5; the Emmons County Record (A14) rewrote that dispatch three weeks later and its dates appear to be its own reworking. The Brainerd wire's arrival time (A5) fits a night of Dec. 5-6 or a delay in its filing.

versions.value: Shackled together and driven off rapidly in a carriage about 6 p.m.; destination unknown, rumored St. Paul
Taken by team across country during the night to the Brainerd jail

conflicts.note: The later reports (A4, A5) settled the destination as Brainerd.
At his arrest he reportedly also gave the name Dassell (A2).
